job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

passage: In our science lab today, we investigated the composition and properties of soil. We started by placing dry soil in a beaker and pouring water over it. Bubbles immediately rose to the surface, proving that soil contains trapped air within its spaces. Next, we examined soil samples under a microscope. We observed that soil is not just powdered rock; it is a complex mixture of weathered rock particles, decaying organic matter called humus, minerals, and living organisms. We then tested different soil types for water percolation. We discovered that percolation is the process of water moving down through the soil, which is distinct from the total amount of water the soil can hold. Finally, we studied a soil profile. We learned that the topsoil is rich in humus and nutrients, making it the most fertile layer, while the layers deeper down near the bedrock are less suitable for plant growth. We also discussed how plant roots actually prevent soil erosion by binding the soil particles together, acting like a net that keeps the earth in place during heavy rains. This experiment showed us that soil is a dynamic, living system essential for agriculture, where specific crops require specific soil types to thrive based on their unique mineral and water-holding needs.

items.evidence: Bubbles immediately rose to the surface, proving that soil contains trapped air within its spaces.
items.q: Water is poured on dry soil and bubbles rise. What does this show?
options: Air was trapped in gaps in the soil
The soil is made only of tiny rocks
The soil was boiling from the water
Water pushes humus up to the top
items.explain: Bubbles rising proves the soil holds trapped air in its spaces.

wrong.why: thinks soil is only rock pieces with nothing else
invents a heating cause for bubbles
thinks soil is solid, so bubbles must come from something else

items.evidence: We learned that percolation is the process of water moving down through the soil, which is distinct from the total amount of water the soil can hold.
items.q: Two soils differ in how fast water passes down through them. What does this compare?
options: Their percolation, not their water-holding amount
Their water-holding amount, not their percolation
Their absorption, which is the same as percolation
Their fertility, which depends on the depth
items.explain: Percolation is water moving down through soil, which is different from how much water soil can hold.

wrong.why: thinks fast percolation means more soaking up of water
thinks percolation and absorption are the same
links soil properties to digging depth

items.evidence: We learned that the topsoil is rich in humus and nutrients, making it the most fertile layer, while the layers deeper down near the bedrock are less suitable for plant growth.
items.q: Why is topsoil better for growing plants than layers near the bedrock?
options: It has more humus and nutrients
It is deeper and so more fertile
It is softer mud, like the lowest layer
It has more water poured on it
items.explain: Topsoil is rich in humus and nutrients, so it is the most fertile layer.

wrong.why: thinks deeper soil is more fertile
thinks deep layers are soft mud
thinks water alone makes soil good for plants

items.evidence: We also discussed how plant roots actually prevent soil erosion by binding the soil particles together, acting like a net that keeps the earth in place during heavy rains.
items.q: A hill's plants are cut down before heavy rains. What will most likely happen?
options: More soil will be washed away
Roots will break rocks into more soil
The soil will stay since no people live there
The soil will bind itself into a net
items.explain: Roots bind soil like a net, so without plants heavy rain washes away more soil.

wrong.why: thinks roots cause erosion by breaking rocks
thinks erosion only happens where people are absent
takes the net image literally, reversing cause

items.evidence: This experiment showed us that soil is a dynamic, living system essential for agriculture, where specific crops require specific soil types to thrive based on their unique mineral and water-holding needs.
items.q: Which example best shows that crops need specific soil types?
options: A crop fails in soil lacking its minerals
A crop grows well in any soil with water
A crop grows better in deeper soil layers
A crop fails in soil that holds air
items.explain: Crops need specific minerals and water-holding ability, so a crop fails if the soil lacks them.

wrong.why: thinks any crop grows in any soil with water
thinks deeper soil is always better
thinks air in soil is harmful
